terms.def: Annual Percentage Rate. The yearly interest rate on borrowed money. Divide by 12 for the monthly rate.
Someone allowed to use another person's credit card account. Can help a teen start building credit history.
A bank setting that moves money (for example, to savings) on a schedule without you doing anything.
How much money is in an account, or how much you owe on a card or loan.
A plan for where every dollar of your income goes.
A bank account for everyday spending: paychecks in, debit card and bills out.
Interest earned on your original money and on interest you already earned. Makes savings grow faster over time.
A card that lets you borrow money up to a limit. You pay it back later, with interest if you don't pay in full.
The most you're allowed to owe on a credit card.
A record of how you've borrowed and repaid money. You can check yours for free.
A number from about 300 to 850 that shows lenders how likely you are to repay. Higher is better.
A bank owned by its members. Often has lower fees.
A card that spends money straight from your checking account.
Money you owe and have to pay back.
Paying off debts from highest APR to lowest. Usually saves the most interest.
Paying off debts from smallest balance to largest, rolling each finished payment into the next debt.
Money taken out of your paycheck, like taxes.
The day a bill must be paid to avoid late fees.
Savings kept only for real surprises, like car repairs or losing a job.
A U.S. government agency that insures bank deposits up to $250,000.
Social Security (6.2%) and Medicare (1.45%) taken from your paycheck.
A cost that stays the same each month, like rent or a phone plan.
Time between your statement and due date, on cards that have one. Pay the full statement balance by the due date and you pay no interest on purchases.
Your pay before taxes and deductions.
Money coming in: paychecks, allowance, gifts, side gigs.
The cost of borrowing money, or the money a bank pays you for saving.
The smallest amount you can pay on a card or loan without a late fee.
Something you must have to live, work, or stay safe.
Take-home pay after taxes and deductions.
What you give up when you choose to spend money on one thing instead of another.
Spending more than you have in checking. Often comes with a fee.
A fee (often around $35) a bank charges when it covers a purchase you didn't have money for.
The paper or online record that shows your gross pay, each deduction, and your net pay.
Money your employer pays you for work, usually every week or two.
The amount you borrowed, not counting interest.
A bank account for money you aren't spending yet. Pays interest.
A starter credit card where your cash deposit becomes your credit limit.
Your monthly credit card bill, showing purchases, balance, minimum payment, and due date.
Your card balance divided by your credit limit. 30% is a common guideline, not a cutoff: lower is better.
A cost that changes from month to month, like groceries or gas.
The form you fill out at a new job that sets how much federal tax is withheld.
Something nice to have that you could live without.
Tax your employer holds back from each paycheck and sends to the government for you.
A budget guide, not a rule: 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings.
